segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Welcome the one who is weak in faith, but not to pass judgment on his opinions.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who eats must not look down on the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who are you to judge someone else’s household servant? Before his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One person judges one day to be above another; another judges every day to be alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord. And the one who eats, eats for the Lord, since he gives thanks to God; and the one who does not eat, it is for the Lord that he does not eat, and he gives thanks to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If we live, we live for the Lord, and if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is why Christ died and came to life: so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you—why do you judge your brother? Or you—why do you look down on your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow to me, and every tongue will give praise to God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So each of us will give an account of himself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So let us no longer judge one another. Make this your judgment instead: not to put a stumbling block or a trap in your brother’s way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; but to the one who considers something unclean, to that person it is unclean.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not by your food destroy the one for whom Christ died.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not let the good that is yours be slandered.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the one who serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, let us pursue what makes for peace and for building one another up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not tear down the work of God for the sake of food. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for the person whose eating is a stumbling block.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything by which your brother stumbles or is made to fall or is weak.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The faith that you have, keep to yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because it is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.

notes.phrase: but not to pass judgment on his opinions
notes.traditional: but not to quarrel over opinions
notes.note: The Greek phrase is compressed and can be read two ways. The noun usually means evaluating or distinguishing, which gives “passing judgment on opinions” and fits the chapter’s repeated warnings against judging. It can also mean a dispute, and most modern translations take it that way: “not for quarrels over opinions.”

“Master” here and “the Lord” in the next sentence are the same Greek word. Paul moves from the picture of a household servant answerable only to his own master to the believer’s Lord, and the wordplay continues through verse 9.

The earliest manuscripts read “of God”; many later ones, followed by the King James Version, read “of Christ,” probably under the influence of 2 Corinthians 5:10. The word for “judgment seat” is the raised platform from which a magistrate heard cases.

Paul quotes Isaiah 45:23 in its Greek form, with an opening formula found in Isaiah 49:18. In the Greek Scriptures this verb with “to God” regularly means to acknowledge God openly with praise or thanks, as often in the Psalms. “Confess to God” now suggests admitting sins, which is not the point; some translations have “acknowledge God.”

notes.traditional: give account of himself to God
notes.note: Many manuscripts, and most English translations, add “to God” at the end of the sentence. Some important early witnesses lack the words, and the Greek text followed here omits them. The meaning is not affected, since verse 10 has already named God’s judgment seat.

notes.traditional: hindrance, obstacle, or occasion to fall
notes.note: Paul pairs two near-synonyms for something that brings a person down. The second word is rendered “stumbling block” elsewhere in this translation, but here that wording is taken by the first word, so “trap” is used—a sense the word has in the Greek Scriptures. Most translations have “hindrance” or “obstacle,” which are milder than the Greek.

The Greek word ordinarily means “common” or “shared.” Among Greek-speaking Jews it had come to mean ritually defiled, the opposite of holy or clean, and was used especially of food forbidden by the Law or tainted by contact with what was forbidden. Paul’s point concerns ritual status, not hygiene.

Paul does not say what “your good” is. Most interpreters take it as the freedom of the strong to eat anything, which would be brought into disrepute if it harmed others. Others take it as the gospel or the blessings the whole community shares. The verb is the one traditionally transliterated “blaspheme,” which in Greek covered defamatory speech of any kind.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice). Here most interpreters take the word to mean right conduct toward others in the community. Some take it as the right standing with God that Paul has described earlier in the letter.

notes.phrase: whose eating is a stumbling block
notes.note: The Greek is literally “the person who eats through a stumbling block.” This translation takes it of the strong believer whose eating trips up someone else, which suits the commands on either side. It can also be read of the weak believer who eats against his own conscience and so stumbles himself, as in verse 23.

notes.phrase: or is made to fall or is weak
notes.traditional: or is offended, or is made weak
notes.note: Several early manuscripts end the sentence at “stumbles,” and most modern translations follow them. The Greek text translated here includes the longer reading, which is also early and widely attested. “Is made to fall” renders a verb the King James Version translates “is offended”; it refers to being brought down in one’s faith, not to hurt feelings.

In this context “faith” is the settled confidence before God that a particular action is permitted, as in verses 2 and 22. Most interpreters therefore take the closing sentence as a statement about acting against one’s own conviction. It has also long been read as a general principle that whatever does not spring from Christian faith is sin.

candidates.reason: Used throughout the letters for a fellow believer of either sex; translations split between “brother” and “brother or sister,” and the choice should be uniform.
It is paired with σκάνδαλον here and in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8, so its rendering must be fixed in coordination with the σκάνδαλον entry.
The ritual sense (Mark 7, Acts 10–11, Romans 14, Hebrews 10:29) is rendered variously as “common,” “unclean,” “defiled” or “profane,” and needs to be distinguished consistently from ἀκάθαρτος.
The middle/passive is traditionally “doubt” (Matthew 21:21, Romans 4:20, James 1:6), but “waver” or “be divided” has strong lexical support and the choice should be uniform.
The figurative sense of conducting one’s life recurs across Paul and John, and translations vary between “walk,” “live” and “behave.”
